title: Thinking locally: Reflections on Dynamical Mean-Field Theory from a high-temperature/high-energy perspective

Thinking locally: Reflections on Dynamical Mean-Field Theory from a high-temperature/high-energy perspective
Antoine Georges $^{1,2,3,*}$
$^{1}$ Collège de France, 11 place Marcelin Berthelot, 75005 Paris, France
$^{2}$ Centre de Physique Théorique, Ecole Polytechnique, CNRS, 91128 Palaiseau Cedex, France
$^{3}$ Université de Genève, DPMC, 24 quai Ernest Ansermet, 1211 Geneva 4, Switzerland
Received 20 February 2011, accepted 6 March 2011 by T. Pruschke Published online 13 September 2011
Key words Strongly correlated systems, Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, cold atoms, Mott transition, high-temperature series.
This article is dedicated to Dieter Vollhardt on the occasion of his 60th birthday.

When spatial correlations are short-range, the physics of strongly correlated systems is controlled by local quantum fluctuations. In those regimes, Dynamical Mean-Field Theory can be viewed as a 'compass' which provides guidance on the relevant degrees of freedom and their effective dynamics over intermediate energy scales. These intermediate energy scales and associated crossovers play a crucial role in the physics of strongly correlated materials.

Over the past two decades, Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) has had considerable impact on our understanding of the physics of strongly correlated quantum systems, both in the context of simplified models and of real materials [1,

2].

To appreciate the significance of DMFT, we must first understand the landscape it revolutionized.

At the heart of this approach is the representation of the local spectral function of the solid as that of an atom self-consistently embedded into an effective medium. This is a deep change of paradigm as compared to more traditional approaches in solid-state
a solid as an inhomogeneous electron gas, to which interactions
as a perturbation. This "gas-like" view treats electrons as if they are primarily free particles moving through a background, with interactions being a secondary correction.

In contrast, DMFT gives central importance to the fact that, after all, solids are made of atoms (!) and that an isolated atom is a small many-body problem in itself which must be properly described from the start.

Think of it this way: instead of starting with a smooth fluid and trying to add "bumps" for interactions, DMFT starts with the discrete, complex structure of the atom and then asks how it behaves when placed in a crowd.

In strongly-correlated materials, electrons are hesitant entities with a dual character: at high-energy they behave as localized, while at low-energy (in metallic systems) they may eventually form itinerant quasiparticles, albeit with a strongly suppressed spectral weight.

dual nature is the central puzzle of strongly correlated physics. Imagine an electron in a material like a heavy metal oxide. If you probe it with high energy (short time scales), it looks like it is stuck on a specific atom, unable to move freely. This is the "localized" aspect. However, if you look at low energies (long time scales), these electrons can cooperate to form collective excitations called quasiparticles that move through the lattice, though they are sluggish and "heavy" compared to free electrons.

In such systems, the local atomic point of view is therefore a particularly meaningful starting point, with a built-in real-space description of the atomic multiplets and of their broadening in the solid.

The term "atomic multiplets" refers to the various energy states an atom can have due to the spin and orbital interactions of its electrons. By starting locally, DMFT naturally captures these complex internal structures.

As to low-energy quasiparticles, their description is made possible in this approach by the hybridization with the effective medium, which may screen the atomic multiplets through a Kondo-like process.

Here, the "effective medium" acts as a bath of other electrons. The "hybridization" is the coupling between the local atom and this bath. The "Kondo-like process" is a fascinating quantum phenomenon where the local magnetic moment of the atom is "screened" or neutralized by the conduction electrons in the medium, allowing the system to behave as a metal at very low temperatures.

The dual nature of the electron in strongly-correlated materials is also a manifestation of the particle-wave duality: real-space (appropriate for high-energy atomic-like excitations) and momentum-space (appropriate for low-energy quasiparticle excitations) descriptions are reconciled within DMFT.

This reconciliation is a major strength of DMFT. In quantum mechanics, particles are often described either by their position (real-space) or their momentum (wave-like properties). Traditional theories often struggle to switch between these views seamlessly. DMFT bridges this gap: it uses real-space logic to handle the high-energy, localized atomic behavior, and momentum-space logic to handle the low-energy, delocalized quasiparticle behavior.

Together with a representation of the local spectral function, the self-consistent effective atom (quantum impurity) also allows for the calculation of a local self-energy. Within DMFT, this self-energy is identified with that of the full lattice or solid. This is precisely where an approximation is made, while in contrast

the quantum impurity representation of the local spectral function can be viewed as exact. The frequency dependence of this local self-energy is in general quite complex, capturing both high-energy atomic multiplets and low-energy quasiparticles as well as a rich physics of crossovers between these entities as a function of energy and temperature. It is however, local in real space, i.e. momentum-independent $^{1}$ .

This sounds like a very drastic approximation, and it is therefore a legitimate and important question to ask when this approximation is reasonable i.e when momentum dependence can be safely neglected. It is hardly possible to review this issue extensively here. Rather, this short note will present a few miscellaneous reflections. I will in particular emphasize that the local approximation becomes legitimate at high temperature or high energy. This is of course clear both on an intuitive basis and from the general principles of statistical mechanics, but this point of view has perhaps not been emphasized enough. Conceptually, it establishes DMFT as a sort of compass which can guide us towards the correct physical modelling on an intermediate energy scale. Of course, single-site DMFT must be supplemented by more sophisticated tools when dealing with lower energy scales/longer length scales.
2 Validating DMFT at high temperature: theoretical considerations and experiments with cold atoms
2.1 Conceptual links between high-temperature expansions and mean-field theories

Actually, any mean-field theory in statistical mechanics has strong conceptual links with the limit of high-temperature. In [3], it was shown that mean-field theories of classical spin models can be viewed as a high-temperature expansion of the free-energy considered as a functional of the order parameter (obtained by a Legendre transformation from the energy in an external field), i.e an expansion in powers of $\beta J$ at fixed magnetizations $m_{i}$ (with $\beta = 1/kT$ and J the exchange coupling).

To be specific, consider the Ising model $H = -\sum_{\langle ij\rangle} J_{ij} S_i S_j$ . The free-energy functional A can be written as:
$$
- \beta A [ \{m _ {i} \}; \beta J _ {i j} ] = \sum_ {i} \Gamma_ {\mathrm{loc}} [ m _ {i} ] + \Gamma_ {J} [ \{m _ {i} \}; \beta J _ {i j} ] \tag {1}
$$
In this expression, the local part of the functional corresponds to the entropy of independent spins with constrained magnetizations:
$$
\Gamma_ {\mathrm{loc}} [ m _ {i} ] = - \left[ \frac {1 + m _ {i}}{2} \ln \frac {1 + m _ {i}}{2} + \frac {1 - m _ {i}}{2} \ln \frac {1 - m _ {i}}{2} \right] \tag {2}
$$
and $\Gamma_J$ sums up all the non-local contributions to the functional due to the non-local interaction $J_{ij}$ . Given the exact form of the functional $\Gamma_J$ , the equilibrium magnetizations of the system are obtained from $\delta \Gamma / \delta m_i = 0$ and hence are the solutions of $m_i = \tanh \frac{\delta \Gamma_J}{\delta m_i}$ . From this equation, it is seen that $\beta^{-1} \delta \Gamma_J / \delta m_i$ can be viewed as the exact self-consistent Weiss field, such that $m_i = \tanh \beta h_i$ .

The mean-field approximation for the Ising model with uniform couplings (e.g. ferromagnetic) $J_{ij} = J$ correspond to a truncation of the functional $\Gamma_{J}$ to its first-order contribution in $\beta J$ , namely:
$$
\Gamma_ {J} ^ {\mathrm{MFT,ferro}} = \beta J \sum_ {\langle i j \rangle} m _ {i} m _ {j} \tag {3}
$$
Hence, the familiar mean-field equation $m_{i} = \tanh \beta \sum_{j} J_{ij} m_{j}$ . This approximation becomes exact in the limit of large dimensions (lattice connectivity). In this limit, the exchange has to be scaled as $J = J^{*}/d$ , and only the two terms (2), (3) survive in the large-d limit.

2.2 Benchmarking DMFT at high temperature
Recently, motivated

by experiments on fermionic atoms in optical lattices, a systematic comparison between high-temperature series for the Hubbard model on a three-dimensional cubic lattice [9] and the corresponding DMFT approximation has been performed [10].

understand the significance of this comparison, let's first break down the components. The **Hubbard model** is a fundamental theoretical framework used to describe the behavior of electrons (or atoms) moving on a lattice, where they interact with each other when they occupy the same site. In this specific study, the researchers are looking at a **three-dimensional cubic lattice**, which is a grid of points arranged in a cube, much like a 3D version of a chessboard.

The comparison involves two distinct methods:
1.  **High-temperature series:** This is a mathematical technique used to approximate the behavior of a system when thermal energy is high enough that particles are moving rapidly and interactions are less dominant. It provides a benchmark for how the system should behave in this regime.
2.  **DMFT (Dynamical Mean-Field Theory) approximation:** This is the primary method being tested. DMFT is a powerful tool that simplifies the complex many-body problem by focusing on local interactions while retaining the full frequency dependence of the electron's motion. It is designed to be exact in the limit of infinite dimensions, but its accuracy in realistic 3D systems needs to be verified.

The goal of this systematic comparison is to validate the DMFT approximation by checking if its predictions match the results from the high-temperature series, which serves as a reliable reference point in that specific temperature range.

In a nutshell, these comparisons fully support the intuitive view that physics become more local in space as temperature is raised (because the correlation lengths for any kind of short-range ordering become very short), so that single-site DMFT is a quantitatively accurate approach in those regimes. Because it involves a partial resummation of the high-temperature series, it can be used down to lower temperature than the series for a large range of densities, and furthermore allows for a direct calculation of frequency-dependent response functions.
2.3 Benchmarking DMFT in cold atom experiments
A direct quantitative comparison with experiments in this high-temperature range is hardly possible in the solid-state context, and would anyhow be complicated by phonon degrees of freedom. Experiments with cold atomic gases trapped in optical lattices offer however a beautiful opportunity. The rapid development of experimental techniques in this field allows for the engineering of artificial solids with a high degree of controllability, opening a new field of research to explore strongly correlated phases of quantum systems in a new context. Key steps along this path have of course been the theoretical proposal for realizing Hubbard-like models and observing the Mott transition in this context $[12]$ , and the experimental observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition of bosonic atoms $[13]$ . Recently, the crossover from an itinerant state into a Mott incompressible state as coupling is increased has been observed experimentally in the fermionic case as well $[14, 15]$ . Those experiments have provided us with an ‘analog quantum simulator’ validation of single-site DMFT, admittedly still in a rather high-temperature regime.
Two such comparisons between theory and experimental results are reproduced in Fig. 2. In Fig. 2(a) [16], the measured double occupancy as a function of atom number is compared to theoretical calculations

performed at constant entropy (assuming that turning on the optical lattice corresponds to an adiabatic process).

To understand why this assumption is critical, consider the physics of the experiment: when the optical lattice is switched on, it happens rapidly compared to the timescale of heat exchange with the environment. In thermodynamics, a process that occurs without heat transfer is called *adiabatic*. For an ideal system, an adiabatic process implies that the total entropy of the system remains constant. This is a powerful constraint because it links the initial state of the gas (before the lattice is turned on) to the final state (after the lattice is established).

This agreement is significant because it validates the theoretical framework. If two different mathematical approaches—one based on expanding the system's behavior at high temperatures and the other based on the sophisticated DMFT approximation—produce the same outcome, it gives us high confidence that the underlying physics is being captured correctly.
Fitting theory to experiment allows for a determination of the actual value of the entropy, and ultimately of the temperature attained after the lattice is turned on, for a given particle number.

Here, the "fitting" process acts as a bridge between the abstract world of theory and the concrete data from the lab. By adjusting the theoretical parameters to match the experimental observations, researchers can reverse-engineer the state of the system. Specifically, they can deduce the entropy, which serves as a proxy for the temperature. This is crucial because, in these ultracold atom experiments, direct temperature measurement is often difficult; instead, we infer the temperature from the distribution of particles and their interactions.
This analysis reveals that the lowest temperature that was reached in this experiment (at small atom number) is comparable to the hopping amplitude $T \sim

t$. To grasp the significance of this, we must define the **hopping amplitude**, denoted by $t$. In the context of an optical lattice, atoms are not fixed in place; they can "hop" from one lattice site to a neighboring one due to quantum mechanical tunneling. The parameter $t$ quantifies the energy scale associated with this motion. When the temperature $T$ is comparable to $t$, it means the thermal energy of the atoms is on the same order of magnitude as the energy required for them to move. This is a critical regime: if $T \ll t$, the atoms are highly mobile and delocalized; if $T \gg t$, thermal fluctuations dominate and suppress coherent quantum behavior. Being in the $T \sim
places the system in a delicate balance where both quantum motion and thermal disorder play significant roles.
The regime with very small double occupancy at the two largest values of U/6t actually corresponds to the formation of a Mott plateau in the center of the trap.

Let's unpack this. **Double occupancy** refers to the probability of finding two atoms on the same lattice site. In a system with strong repulsive interactions (high $U$, the on-site interaction energy), atoms try to avoid sharing a site. When the ratio of interaction energy to hopping energy ($U/t$) is large, the system resists double occupancy. A **Mott plateau** is a region in the density profile where the number of particles per site remains constant (typically an integer, like 1) despite changes in the chemical potential or local density conditions. This happens because the system becomes incompressible: it is energetically costly to add or remove a particle from a site that is already occupied, due to the strong repulsion $U$. The observation of this plateau in the center of the trap is a hallmark of the Mott insulating phase, where the system behaves like an insulator not because of band structure, but because of electron-electron (or atom-atom) correlations.

This is more clearly revealed in the measurement of the cloud size as a function of trap compression (Fig. 2b [15]) as a plateau signalling the onset of an incompressible regime for the largest value of U displayed.

The "cloud size" refers to the spatial extent of the atomic gas. In a compressible gas, if you compress the trap (make it tighter), the cloud shrinks significantly. However, in an incompressible Mott insulator, the density is fixed, so the cloud size does not shrink as easily; it forms a plateau in the size-versus-compression graph. This visual signature is a direct experimental confirmation of the incompressibility predicted by the Mott physics.

Progress in cooling techniques will undoubtedly allow one to reach lower temperatures in future experiments. In this context, it will be quite interesting to document deviations from single-site DMFT as longer-range correlations develop, and to benchmark theoretical calculations including these effects, such as cluster extensions of single-site DMFT (see below).

As we cool the system further, the limitations of the **single-site DMFT** approximation become apparent. Single-site DMFT assumes that the only important correlations are those occurring on a single lattice site (local correlations). It treats the rest of the lattice as an average background. However, as temperature drops, **longer-range correlations** emerge. These are correlations between particles on different sites that are not just nearest neighbors but extend over several lattice spacings. To capture these effects, theorists use **cluster extensions of DMFT**, where instead of considering a single site, the theory considers a small cluster of sites (e.g., a 2x2 or 3x3 block) and solves the problem exactly within that cluster, while still approximating the rest of the lattice. This allows the theory to account for spatial correlations that single-site DMFT misses.

As temperature is lowered, the range of spatial correlations (as measured by the correlation length for the various types of short-range order) increases, and corrections to single-site DMFT become increasingly important. Here, I briefly review some physical consequences, focusing on the physics associated with the proximity of a Mott transition.

3.2 Pomeranchuk effect and the metal-insulator critical boundary

The entropy of the insulating phase has also direct relevance for the shape of the critical boundary separating the metal from the insulating phase in materials which are poised close to the Mott transition. Indeed, the entropy in the metallic phase at low temperature is limited by the Fermi statistics of the quasiparticles and the Pauli principle, and hence linear in temperature $S \sim \gamma T$ (possibly with an enhanced value of $\gamma$ , see below). As a result, if the insulating phase is a localized paramagnet with short-range spatial correlations and a high entropy per site, it becomes possible to gain a lot of free-energy by taking advantage of this entropy and localize the particles upon heating. This is the Pomeranchuk effect, which explains why liquid Helium 3 (a spin-1/2 fermion) can be solidified upon heating at high pressure, while this phenomenon is not observed for liquid Helium 4 (a spinless boson). For this reason, the metallic phase of $V_{2}O_{3}$ can be turned into a Mott insulator upon heating, as manifested by the negative slope $dT_{MIT}/dp > 0$ of the (first-order) metal-insulator critical boundary as a function of pressure (Fig. 4a). This is in agreement with the observation of local moments in the insulating phase, with an enhanced Curie-Weiss law for the magnetic susceptibility. It is interesting to contrast this observation to the phase diagram of two-dimensional organics of the $\kappa$ -BEDT family (Fig. 4b). These materials also display a first-order metal-insulator transition. In a restricted temperature range of temperature below the critical endpoint, the slope of the critical boundary is again positive, as for $V_{2}O_{3}$ , but turns around into $dT_{MIT}/dp < 0$ for $T \lesssim 30 K$ . This can be interpreted as due to antiferromagnetic correlations of increasing range, which quenches the entropy of the insulator so that the ‘Pomeranchuk effect’ does not apply any more. This observation suggests that using single-site DMFT (while taking into account the actual electronic structure of the material) to describe the metal-insulator transition of $V_{2}O_{3}$ at temperatures around the critical endpoint $T_{c} \simeq 450 K$ but also significantly below that scale is quite reasonable (as indeed has been done successfully [21–25]). In contrast, the range of applicability of single-site DMFT is probably more limited for the organic materials when considering the low pressure regime close to the insulating phase.

3.4 Magnetic correlations and the effective mass of quasiparticles

Now, let us shift our focus to a different but related consequence of magnetic correlations: the behavior of the **effective mass** of quasiparticles.

**What is a Quasiparticle?**

In a solid, electrons do not move freely like they do in a vacuum. They interact with the lattice and with each other. A "quasiparticle" is a mathematical construct that represents an electron dressed in all these interactions. Its "effective mass" ($m^*$) tells us how hard it is to accelerate this dressed electron. A heavy effective mass means the electron moves sluggishly, as if it were much heavier than a free electron.
